sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Every fullstack role involves wiring a frontend to a backend over HTTP. Interviewers test whether you know which HTTP verb to use, why CORS blocks you, and how to handle errors gracefully on both sides. Getting these fundamentals right is what separates a developer who can ship features from one who is perpetually blocked.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body:
- **HTTP method** encodes intent: GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH edits, DELETE removes.
- **Safe** = no side-effects (GET, HEAD). **Idempotent** = multiple identical calls = same result as one call (GET, PUT, DELETE).
- **CORS** is a browser security policy: the server must explicitly tell the browser which origins are allowed.
- **fetch** is native but verbose; **axios** adds interceptors, automatic JSON parsing, and proper error throwing.
- **Jackson** on the Spring side and **JSON.parse/stringify** on the JS side do the same job — translate between objects and JSON strings.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
- HTTP Methods: know safe vs idempotent matrix cold.
- Fetch vs Axios: fetch does NOT throw on 4xx/5xx — you must check response.ok.
- CORS: preflight OPTIONS fires before cross-origin requests with non-simple headers/methods.
- Jackson: camelCase Java field → camelCase JSON by default; configure @JsonNaming for snake_case APIs.
- Error handling: distinguish network error (fetch rejects) from HTTP error (fetch resolves with 4xx/5xx).
- Loading states: always model three states — loading, error, success — never assume success.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
- "What is the difference between PUT and PATCH?" → PUT replaces the entire resource (idempotent); PATCH applies a partial update.
- "Why does my React app get a CORS error?" → Browser enforces Same-Origin Policy; Spring must respond with correct Access-Control-Allow-Origin header.
- "Why would you use axios over fetch?" → Axios throws on 4xx/5xx, has request/response interceptors, and parses JSON automatically.
- "How does the Authorization header work?" → Client sends 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' with every protected request; server validates it.
- "What happens during a preflight request?" → Browser sends OPTIONS first to check server permissions; server must respond with CORS headers or request is blocked.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: > *"When my React app calls a Spring Boot API, the browser first checks if the origins match. If they don't, it sends a preflight OPTIONS request. Spring Boot must respond with Access-Control-Allow-Origin set to my frontend's origin. On the client side, I prefer axios because it automatically parses JSON and throws errors on 4xx and 5xx responses, which I can catch in a global interceptor. I model every API call with three states — loading, error, and success — so the user always knows what's happening."*
